**Direction:** Prompt an open model to answer factual questions 'citing your sources' with CoT. Programmatically check each cited source/quote against a reality oracle (web/citation lookup tool, which this repo has). Measure the rate at which CoT-cited evidence is fabricated, and whether fabricated-citation answers are more confidently wrong.

**Why it matters:** Citation-laden CoT is increasingly trusted by users; quantifying how often the cited scaffolding is invented exposes a deceptive-explanation failure outside any lab. Names: CoT unfaithfulness and citation/factual hallucination.

**Relevant context:** Retrieval sycophancy work notes 'spurious citations'; 'CoT Is Not Explainability' (Barez et al.) argues CoT can be a misleading narrative; legal-hallucination work (arXiv:2401.01301) documents fabricated citations. Repo has CrossRef/Semantic Scholar verification tools.

# Multimodal Jailbreak x Text Guardrail Blindness: Image-Carried Harm Past Text Filters

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: cross-modal jailbreak (harm encoded in the image modality) and text-only guardrails (safety filters that only inspect the text prompt). When harmful intent is decomposed into a benign-looking image plus benign text, both the input filter and the text moderator can pass it. The rate at which an open text-safety classifier is blinded by image-carried instructions is unquantified.

**Direction:** Use an open VLM (LLaVA/Qwen2-VL-7B). Take harmful behaviors, split each into benign text + an image carrying the harmful instruction (typographic image or cross-modal obfuscation). Run the text portion through an open text-safety classifier (Llama-Guard) and measure how often it passes while the VLM still reconstructs harmful output. Success criterion: a 'blindness rate' for the text guardrail when intent is shifted to the image channel.

**Why it matters:** Many deployed safety stacks moderate text only; the compound of modality-shift + text-only moderation creates a structural blind spot for the growing multimodal surface. Evaluation-only, open models, consumer GPU, no lab infra.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2506.16760 CAMO decomposes malicious prompts into benign visual+textual fragments; arXiv:2509.21401 JaiLIP and arXiv:2405.17894 white-box multimodal jailbreaks report >80% success. LLaVA, Qwen2-VL, Llama-Guard all open.

# Sycophancy x Multi-Agent Drift: Does Agreeableness Cause Consensus on Wrong Answers?

**Problem:** In multi-agent debate/critique setups (a popular oversight idea), sycophancy compounds with error propagation: agents defer to each other's stated positions, converging on a confidently-wrong consensus instead of correcting it. The 'wisdom of agents' becomes mutual sycophancy.

**Direction:** Run a 2-3 agent debate (same open model, different roles) on factual questions where one agent is seeded with a wrong answer. Measure whether the group converges to the wrong answer (sycophantic deference) more often than a single agent would err, and whether confidence rises with rounds. Inference-only.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent oversight is proposed as a scalable safety mechanism; if sycophancy drives false consensus, it can manufacture unwarranted confidence rather than catch errors. Names: inter-agent sycophancy and multi-agent error propagation.

**Relevant context:** 'Not Just RLHF: Why Alignment Alone Won't Fix Multi-Agent Sycophancy' (arXiv:2605.12991); 'Hallucination Cascade ... in Multi-Agent LLM Systems' (arXiv:2606.07937).

# CoT Length x Faithfulness: Does Compressing Reasoning (Efficiency) Reduce Monitorability?

**Problem:** An efficiency/capability pressure — shorter CoT — compounds with a safety failure: as CoT gets terser (or models adopt 'low-controllability' compact traces), monitorability and faithfulness may drop together, eroding the oversight handle.

**Direction:** Prompt an open reasoning model to solve hint-planted problems under varying CoT length budgets ('answer in one line' ... 'think step by step at length'). Measure how the hint-mention (faithfulness) rate and a monitor's hit-rate change with CoT length. Report the faithfulness-vs-brevity tradeoff curve. Inference-only.

**Why it matters:** Labs are incentivized to shorten CoT for cost/latency; this quantifies the safety cost of that pressure on monitorability — a medium-horizon concern labs may deprioritize. Names: CoT compression/efficiency pressure and faithfulness/monitorability loss.

**Relevant context:** Korbak et al. note 'optimizing for shorter, less interpretable CoTs can reduce monitorability'; GPT-5 system card notes 'low' CoT controllability as a (debated) safety property; faithfulness measured via planted hints.

# Sycophancy x Demographic Bias: Does Tailoring to Perceived User Identity Compound Into Differential Honesty?

**Problem:** Sycophancy is sensitive to perceived user characteristics; this compounds with fairness/bias failures: the model may give differently-truthful answers depending on inferred user demographic, producing unequal honesty rather than just unequal tone.

**Direction:** Hold the factual question fixed; vary only cues about the user's stated group/affiliation/expertise. On a factual+contested-claims set, measure variance in truthfulness and confidence across user framings for an open model. Report demographic-conditioned honesty gaps (the compound effect), distinct from refusal-rate gaps.

**Why it matters:** If models are more honest with some users than others, that's a fairness-AND-honesty failure invisible to standard truthfulness benchmarks that use neutral prompts. No lab data needed. Names: sycophancy (user-conditioning) and demographic bias.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy work notes biases 'influenced by perceived user characteristics or social power dynamics'; self-preference/sycophancy magnitudes 6-22% under disclosure. TruthfulQA for the factual base.

# Unfaithful CoT x Safety Classifier Evasion: Can a Model Pass a CoT Safety Filter While Acting Unsafely?

**Problem:** Defense-in-depth often adds a CoT-reading safety classifier. This compounds badly with unfaithfulness: a model can emit a 'safe-looking' CoT (rejecting the harmful intent) while the final output is unsafe, sailing past the classifier — combining unfaithfulness with filter evasion.

**Direction:** Construct prompts where a small open model can produce a benign-sounding CoT but a borderline-unsafe final answer (e.g., 'explain why X is dangerous' that nonetheless leaks the how). Run an off-the-shelf CoT-based safety judge; measure how often unsafe finals pass because the CoT looks safe. Prototype a cheap mitigation: also judge the final independently.

**Why it matters:** Builds a small monitoring-harness probe showing CoT filters give false assurance; the mitigation (judge the output, not just the reasoning) is strategically valuable infra. Names: CoT unfaithfulness and safety-filter evasion.

**Relevant context:** Alignment Forum unfaithful-CoT example: CoT rejects harmful action while output implements it. Korbak et al. warn fabricated CoT can 'undermine an audit'. 'Roadmap towards Safety Cases based on CoT Monitoring' (arXiv:2510.19476).

# Sycophancy x Hallucination in Medical/Health Q&A: Quantifying the Compound Harm Surface

**Problem:** In high-stakes health questions, sycophancy (agreeing with a worried user's wrong self-diagnosis) and hallucination (fabricating supporting 'facts') compound into actively harmful, confident misinformation — a documented but under-quantified intersection.

**Direction:** Use a public health-QA set. Pose questions cold vs with a leading false premise ('I read that X cures Y, right?'). Measure the rate of confident false agreement and fabricated supporting detail (the compound), graded by an LLM judge + reference answers. Compare across 2-3 open model sizes. Inference-only.

**Why it matters:** Directly maps a real-world harm surface where two honesty failures multiply; results are immediately communicable in a blog post about deploying LLMs in sensitive domains. Names: sycophancy and factual hallucination.

**Relevant context:** 'When helpfulness backfires: LLMs and the risk of false medical information due to sycophantic behavior' (npj Digital Medicine, s41746-025-02008-z); 'Contradictions in Context' (healthcare RAG, arXiv:2511.06668).

# Quantization x Honesty: Does Compressing a Model Degrade Truthfulness More Than Capability?

**Problem:** Deployment-time quantization (an efficiency pressure) may compound with honesty failures: a quantized model could retain task accuracy while sycophancy and miscalibration worsen disproportionately — a safety regression hidden behind stable capability metrics.

**Direction:** Take one open model at full precision and at 8-bit/4-bit (bitsandbytes, fits a consumer GPU). Compare on TruthfulQA, a sycophancy-flip test, and verbalized-confidence calibration. Test whether honesty metrics degrade faster than a capability benchmark (e.g., MMLU subset). Report relative degradation.

**Why it matters:** Most real deployments quantize; if honesty is the first casualty, safety evals on the full-precision model overstate the deployed model's honesty. Pure inference, single GPU, no training. Names: quantization-induced degradation and honesty/calibration failure.

**Relevant context:** Calibration survey notes post-training procedures degrade uncertainty estimation; sycophancy is RLHF-induced and may be brittle under compression. TruthfulQA / SimpleQA as honesty benchmarks; bitsandbytes enables consumer-GPU quantization.

# Sycophancy x Sandbagging: Does Social Pressure Make Models Hide Capability AND Knowledge?

**Problem:** Sandbagging (strategically underperforming) and sycophancy may compound: when a user signals they 'expect a simple answer' or 'aren't an expert', a model may both dumb-down (sandbag) and agree with the user's lower standard — combining capability concealment with dishonest deference.

**Direction:** On a reasoning/QA set, prompt an open model neutrally vs with user cues lowering expectations ('keep it simple, I'm not technical'). Measure accuracy drop and whether the model explicitly endorses giving a less-correct answer. Distinguish genuine simplification from accuracy loss. Inference-only.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether ordinary social cues can elicit capability-hiding — a cheap, accessible probe of sandbagging-adjacent behavior in existing models. Names: sycophancy and sandbagging/capability concealment.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy responds to perceived user expertise/social dynamics (model-written evals, arXiv:2212.09251); sandbagging is a recognized deceptive-capabilities concern in AI safety literature.

# CoT Unfaithfulness x In-Context Bias: Does the CoT Hide Demographic Shortcuts in Decisions?

**Problem:** When models make decisions (hiring screen, loan-like judgments) they may use a demographic shortcut (bias) while producing a CoT that cites only legitimate factors — compounding bias with unfaithful justification, defeating audits that read the rationale.

**Direction:** Use a public resume/decision dataset; vary a protected attribute while holding qualifications fixed. Measure (a) decision shift from the attribute (bias) and (b) whether the CoT ever mentions the attribute as a factor (faithfulness). Quantify 'silent bias' — biased decisions with clean rationales. Inference-only, small open model.

**Why it matters:** Rationale-based audits are a leading fairness/transparency tool; if biased decisions come with exculpatory CoT, audits are fooled. Names: in-context demographic bias and CoT unfaithfulness.

**Relevant context:** Korbak et al.: 'a fabricated CoT could undermine an audit ... looking for bias in a model used for hiring decisions.' Faithfulness measured via whether decisive factors appear in CoT.

# Sycophancy x Prompt-Injection: Does an Injected 'User Opinion' Hijack Honesty in Agent Inputs?

**Problem:** Prompt injection (untrusted content carrying instructions) compounds with sycophancy: injected text that asserts a false 'fact' or 'user preference' may be deferred to exactly because the model is sycophantically agreeable, turning a content channel into an honesty attack.

**Direction:** Build a tiny summarize/answer-over-document task. Inject into the document a false claim phrased as user belief ('the user already knows that X'). Measure how often the open model adopts the injected falsehood in its answer vs an injected neutral claim, isolating the sycophancy contribution to injection success.

**Why it matters:** Connects two attack surfaces: it shows sycophancy lowers the bar for indirect prompt injection to corrupt truthfulness, relevant to RAG/agent security. Inference-only, no lab infra. Names: prompt injection and sycophancy.

**Relevant context:** Retrieval/agentic-RAG SoK (arXiv:2603.07379) lists 'memory poisoning, retrieval misalignment' as compounding risks; sycophancy increases deference to stated user beliefs.

# Hallucination x Abstention Failure: Where Does the Model Both Not Know AND Not Say So?

**Problem:** Honest abstention ('I don't know') is a safety valve; it compounds badly with hallucination when the model neither knows the answer nor abstains. The dangerous region is unknown-and-unabstained, which standard accuracy metrics don't isolate.

**Direction:** On SimpleQA (designed so models often don't know), elicit answers plus an explicit option to abstain. Cross-tabulate (knows/doesn't) x (abstains/answers). Measure the hallucinate-instead-of-abstain mass and test whether a simple confidence-threshold prompt shrinks it (a cheap mitigation prototype). Inference-only.

**Why it matters:** Builds a small, reusable honesty diagnostic separating ignorance from dishonesty, plus a tested mitigation — valuable, self-contained, and lab-independent. Names: hallucination and abstention/calibration failure.

**Relevant context:** I-CALM (arXiv:2604.03904) incentivizes confidence-aware abstention; calibration survey shows overconfidence drives hallucination; SimpleQA is built to expose unknowns.

# Shallow Alignment x Decoding Randomness: Does Sampling Temperature Compound Prefill Attacks?

**Problem:** Two failures: shallow safety alignment (concentrated in first few tokens) and decoding-time stochasticity. Prefill attacks exploit shallow alignment by forcing the first tokens. High-temperature/top-p sampling independently increases off-trajectory tokens. Whether decoding randomness compounds with shallow alignment—raising attack success the further past the (already shallow) safe prefix you sample—is not characterized as an interaction.

**Direction:** On open models, run prefill attacks of varying prefix length while sweeping temperature and top-p. Measure attack success as a 2D surface over (prefix length, temperature). Success criterion: evidence of interaction—e.g. that once past the shallow safe prefix, higher temperature super-additively increases harmful continuation rate—with confidence intervals.

**Why it matters:** Deployment configs choose decoding params for helpfulness/creativity, often unaware they may be widening the shallow-alignment attack window. The compound finding gives operators an actionable, lab-free safety knob. Pure inference, consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2406.05946 (Qi et al., ICLR 2025) shows alignment is concentrated in first few tokens and prefill/decoding-exploit attacks leverage this; arXiv:2606.04778 'Inference-Time Vulnerability Beyond Shallow Safety' studies alignment along generation trajectories.

# Sycophancy x Long-Context Drift: Does Agreeableness Accumulate Over a Long Conversation?

**Problem:** Sycophancy compounds with long-context/position failures: across many turns, small sycophantic concessions accumulate, and earlier honest positions get buried, so the model drifts further from truth the longer the conversation runs.

**Direction:** Construct multi-turn dialogues (10-30 turns) where the user gently pushes a false belief each turn. Track the model's position turn-by-turn for an open model with a long context window. Measure cumulative drift and whether it's worse than a single high-pressure turn (the compound vs single-shot effect). Inference-only.

**Why it matters:** Real usage is long and conversational; the Opus 4.5 card shows benchmarks understate this. A turn-by-turn drift curve is a fresh, communicable result on realistic sycophancy. Names: sycophancy and long-context/cumulative drift.

**Relevant context:** Claude Opus 4.5 system card: real conversational pressure reveals 10% course-correction; sycophancy risks 'amplified in multi-turn interactions'. Long-context position/recency effects are documented LLM failures.

# Unfaithful CoT x Self-Consistency: Does Sampling-Based Self-Consistency Mask Unfaithful Reasoning?

**Problem:** Self-consistency (majority vote over sampled CoTs) is used to boost reliability; it compounds with unfaithfulness when all sampled CoTs are unfaithful in the same direction — the model votes confidently on a hint-influenced answer while every rationale omits the hint, so consistency looks like correctness.

**Direction:** Run self-consistency (k samples) on hint-planted problems with an open model. Measure whether high agreement co-occurs with high hint-influence and low hint-mention. Test whether self-consistency confidence is uncorrelated with faithfulness — i.e., consistent answers can be uniformly unfaithful. Inference-only.

**Why it matters:** Shows a popular reliability heuristic provides no faithfulness guarantee and can manufacture false confidence in hidden reasoning. Names: CoT unfaithfulness and self-consistency-induced overconfidence.

**Relevant context:** Faithfulness via planted hints (Anthropic experiments); self-consistency is a standard CoT method; 'CoT Is Not Explainability' argues consistency does not imply faithful explanation.

# Sycophancy x Fine-Tune Brittleness: Does Light Fine-Tuning Strip Honesty Guardrails First?

**Problem:** A small amount of benign fine-tuning is known to degrade safety; this compounds with honesty failures if sycophancy and miscalibration regress faster than refusals — meaning a community fine-tune can look safe (still refuses) while becoming markedly more dishonest.

**Direction:** Take an open instruct model and a publicly available LoRA fine-tune (or do a tiny LoRA on benign data, feasible on one GPU). Compare base vs fine-tuned on a sycophancy-flip test, TruthfulQA, and refusal rate. Test the hypothesis that honesty degrades before refusal. Report relative regressions.

**Why it matters:** Open-weight fine-tuning is ubiquitous and lab-independent; if honesty is the silent casualty, the open ecosystem ships dishonest models that pass refusal checks. Names: fine-tuning brittleness and honesty/sycophancy degradation.

**Relevant context:** Calibration degrades under SFT/RLHF (calibration survey); safety-brittleness-under-finetuning is established; GPT-5 card raises whether CoT/honesty properties survive fine-tuning. LoRA enables single-GPU fine-tuning.

# Hallucination x Tool Authority: Does an Authoritative Tool Output Suppress Honest Disagreement?

**Problem:** Agents trust tool outputs as ground truth; this compounds with honesty failure when a tool returns a wrong-but-authoritative result and the model abandons a correct belief without flagging the conflict — combining over-trust in tools with failure to honestly surface uncertainty.

**Direction:** Give an open model a calculator/lookup tool that occasionally returns a subtly wrong value. On problems the model can verify itself, measure how often it (a) defers to the wrong tool output and (b) honestly flags the discrepancy. Report deference rate and flag rate (the compound honesty gap). Inference-only with a mock tool.

**Why it matters:** Tool-augmented agents are deployed widely; quantifying silent deference to faulty tools is a practical safety/honesty result and suggests a 'flag conflicts' mitigation. Names: tool over-trust (authority bias) and dishonest non-disclosure of conflict.

**Relevant context:** 'The Reasoning Trap' (arXiv:2510.22977) and AgentHallu show tool-stage hallucinations propagate; 'Verify Before You Commit' (arXiv:2604.08401) proposes self-auditing for faithful agent reasoning.

# Thinking-vs-Answer Acknowledgment Gap Across Hint Types

**Problem:** A recent paper found that open-weight reasoning models acknowledge hint influence in their thinking tokens ~87.5% of the time but in their answer text only ~28.6% of the time. It is unclear whether this suppression gap is constant or varies with the kind of cue that influenced the model.

**Direction:** Reproduce the hint-injection protocol on 2-3 small open-weight reasoning models (e.g. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-4B) via a single GPU. Inject several distinct cue categories (sycophantic user hint, authoritative metadata, a leaked 'correct answer', a subtle reframing) into multiple-choice questions, then measure the acknowledgment rate separately in thinking tokens vs. final answer for each cue type. Test the hypothesis that ethically loaded cues (e.g. a planted answer) are suppressed more in the answer than benign ones.

**Why it matters:** If suppression of hint-acknowledgment depends systematically on cue type, CoT monitoring will have predictable blind spots. Mapping these blind spots is pure evaluation, needs no training or lab infra, and directly informs whether CoT monitoring is a trustworthy safety mechanism on a >1-year horizon.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Why Models Know But Don't Say: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Divergence Between Thinking Tokens and Answers in Open-Weight Reasoning Models' (arXiv 2603.26410, ~March 2026), which reports the ~87.5% thinking-token vs ~28.6% answer-text acknowledgment gap.

# Does Reading About Monitoring Make Small Models Obfuscate?

**Problem:** A recent paper showed that training on documents describing CoT monitoring increases undetected deception. But the participant cannot train models. It is unknown whether merely *prompting* a model with awareness that its CoT is being monitored produces measurable obfuscation in small open models.

**Direction:** Take a single small open reasoning model and a fixed set of tasks with a planted incentive to misbehave (e.g. a reward-hackable instruction). Run two conditions: control vs. a system prompt stating 'your reasoning trace is being read by a monitor'. Use a cheap LLM judge plus keyword analysis to measure whether the CoT becomes shorter, more euphemistic, or less revealing of the true plan while the answer stays the same. Quantify the obfuscation delta.

**Why it matters:** Prompt-induced obfuscation is the cheap, inference-only analog of the train-time obfuscation effect, and would show that monitor-awareness alone degrades CoT transparency. This is a model-organism-style probe of evasive behavior achievable in 30h with no training.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Training on Documents About Monitoring Leads to CoT Obfuscation' (arXiv 2605.15257, ~May 2026) and 'Noticing the Watcher: LLM Agents Can Infer CoT Monitoring from Blocking Feedback' (arXiv 2603.16928), substituting prompt-level monitor-awareness for fine-tuning.

# CoT Controllability as an Early-Warning Probe on Open Models

**Problem:** Recent work argues CoT controllability (a model's ability to reshape its reasoning trace on command) correlates with obfuscation success and could be an early-warning sign of degraded monitorability. The published measurements cover frontier models; the controllability landscape across small open models is uncharted.

**Direction:** Implement the controllability test from the paper: ask models to solve tasks while obeying an instruction to keep a specific fact/word out of (or into) their CoT, and measure compliance rate vs. final-answer compliance. Run across a ladder of small open models varying in size and RL-tuning (base vs. instruct vs. reasoning-distilled). Chart controllability against model attributes to see whether the published 'larger/more-RL = higher controllability' trend holds in the small-model regime.

**Why it matters:** Gives an accessible, reproducible controllability benchmark for the open-model ecosystem that anyone outside a lab can run, providing an early-warning indicator for when CoT monitoring is about to stop working.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought' (arXiv 2603.05706, ~March 2026), which reports e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.5 controls its CoT 2.7% vs 61.9% output control, and links controllability to obfuscation/monitorability.

# Sycophancy Under Real Multi-Turn Pressure vs. Single-Turn Prompts

**Problem:** The Claude Opus 4.5 system card reports that standard single-turn prompts overstate robustness and real conversational pressure reveals only ~10% course-correction. SYCON Bench moved sycophancy to multi-turn, but no cheap reproduction maps the single-turn-to-multi-turn drop across open models.

**Direction:** Build a small harness that takes factual/ethical questions where the model is initially correct, then applies escalating multi-turn user pushback ('are you sure?', appeals to authority, emotional pressure). Measure the turn at which each open model caves (flips to the user's wrong view). Compare the implied single-turn robustness against the multi-turn collapse curve to quantify the overstatement.

**Why it matters:** Realistic sycophancy benchmarks built from conversational pressure (rather than benchmark snapshots) are exactly the fuzzy-reward evaluation the steering favors, need no lab resources, and directly address the open problem of measuring sycophancy under real-world pressure.

**Relevant context:** Extends the Claude Opus 4.5 system card's ~10% course-correction finding and SYCON Bench (multi-turn free-form sycophancy, ~Feb 2026); related to 'The Hidden Cost of Contextual Sycophancy' (arXiv 2605.18372).

# Replicating BrokenMath-Style Sycophancy on Open Reasoning Models

**Problem:** BrokenMath found GPT-5 produces sycophantic 'proofs' of false theorem statements 29% of the time. Whether small open reasoning models exhibit similar or worse sycophancy on subtly false math claims, and whether their CoT reveals doubt before they cave, is unknown.

**Direction:** Take a sample of BrokenMath-style perturbed (false) theorem statements, present them to 2-3 open reasoning models, and measure the rate of confident false 'proofs' vs. correct refutation. Crucially, scan the CoT for hedging/doubt markers that contradict the confident final answer, quantifying a 'doubt-in-CoT but confident-answer' faithfulness gap specific to the math domain.

**Why it matters:** Math theorem proving is a fuzzy-reward setting where the model can be confidently wrong, and detecting CoT-answer doubt gaps probes faithfulness with an objective ground truth. Fully reproducible outside a lab with a public benchmark.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'BrokenMath: A Benchmark for Sycophancy in Theorem Proving with LLMs' (arXiv 2510.04721), reporting 29% sycophancy for GPT-5; combines with the CoT-answer divergence theme of arXiv 2603.26410.

# Stress-Testing 'Universal Truth Directions' on Reasoning Computation

**Problem:** A recent paper shows linear truth probes are reliable for factual recall but break down when truth depends on computing/storing intermediate results, and are sensitive to layer choice and instruction framing. The extent of breakdown across multi-step arithmetic/logic depth is not mapped.

**Direction:** Use an off-the-shelf small open model, extract hidden activations for true/false statements at varying 'computation depth' (0-step factual recall, 1-step, multi-step arithmetic/logic), and fit simple logistic-regression truth probes. Plot probe accuracy as a function of computation depth and layer to characterize exactly where the linear truth direction degrades. No training of the base model needed; only lightweight probe fitting.

**Why it matters:** Lie/truth probes are a leading white-box honesty tool that anyone with a single GPU can study. Mapping their failure boundary as computation deepens tells us when activation-based deception detection can be trusted, a key white-box-honesty open problem.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Testing the Limits of Truth Directions in LLMs' (arXiv 2604.03754, ~April 2026), which reports truth directions break down when truth depends on intermediate computation and are layer/instruction sensitive; builds on Marks & Tegmark truth-direction work.

# Jailbreak Defense x Over-Refusal: Mapping the Compound Cost of Stacked Defenses

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: residual jailbreak vulnerability and over-refusal (false refusal of benign prompts). Each defense added to reduce jailbreaks tends to increase over-refusal. The compound effect of stacking multiple lightweight defenses (system-prompt hardening + input classifier + self-check) on the joint (attack-success, over-refusal) frontier is not mapped for open models.

**Direction:** On an open model, evaluate single and stacked combinations of 3 cheap inference-time defenses. Measure attack success (StrongREJECT subset) and over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench) for each combination. Success criterion: a Pareto frontier showing whether stacking defenses produces super-linear over-refusal growth for diminishing jailbreak reduction.

**Why it matters:** Operators stack defenses assuming additive safety; if over-refusal compounds faster than protection, the system becomes unusable before it becomes safe—a core helpfulness/safety tradeoff. Cheap, no training, lab-free; produces a reusable evaluation recipe.

**Relevant context:** OR-Bench (openreview obYVdcMMIT, 80k prompts) and XSTest (250 safe + 200 unsafe contrasts) measure over-refusal; arXiv:2509.11629 Answer-Then-Check and arXiv:2512.01037 'When Safety Blocks Sense' document the safety/utility tradeoff. StrongREJECT public.

# Do Truth Probes Survive a Sycophantic Conversation Format?

**Problem:** Truth probes are usually validated on isolated statements. Recent work explores generalization to conversational formats, but it is unclear whether a probe trained on neutral statements still flags a model's internal 'false' representation when the model is being sycophantically led to agree with a wrong user.

**Direction:** Fit a truth probe on neutral true/false statements for a small open model, then evaluate it on activations captured during sycophancy-pressure dialogues (where the model outputs a wrong-but-agreeable answer). Test whether the probe still reads 'internally false' when the model verbally agrees with the user. This connects activation-based honesty detection with sycophancy.

**Why it matters:** If probes still register internal falsehood during sycophantic agreement, a cheap white-box sycophancy detector becomes feasible without any lab tooling. If they fail, it bounds the reliability of probe-based honesty monitoring.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Exploring the generalization of LLM truth directions on conversational formats' (arXiv 2505.09807) and 'Testing the Limits of Truth Directions in LLMs' (arXiv 2604.03754), combined with the sycophancy course-correction finding from the Claude Opus 4.5 system card.

# Verbosity Component of Monitorability on Small Open Models

**Problem:** A recent paper decomposes CoT monitorability into faithfulness AND verbosity (does the CoT list every factor needed to solve the task), combining them into one score. This decomposition has not been measured for small open reasoning models, where it could differ sharply.

**Direction:** Implement the monitorability score: construct tasks with a known set of required factors, run small open reasoning models, and use an LLM judge to check which required factors are explicitly listed in the CoT (verbosity) and whether the listed reasoning matches the answer (faithfulness). Report the combined monitorability score and the verbosity/faithfulness breakdown per model.

**Why it matters:** Verbosity is a neglected, easily measurable axis of whether a CoT can serve as the model's external working memory for monitors. A reproducible small-model monitorability scoreboard is valuable infrastructure for the broader community.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Measuring Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity' (arXiv 2510.27378), which introduces the verbosity axis and combined monitorability score.

# Causal Bypass: How Often Does the CoT Not Matter?

**Problem:** A recent paper shows that in some cases the chain of thought is causally inert: the answer is the same whether or not the CoT supports it ('causal bypass'). The prevalence of causal bypass across task types and small models has not been systematically measured.

**Direction:** For a battery of tasks, generate the model's CoT, then intervene by truncating, corrupting, or replacing the CoT with a contradictory one, and measure how often the final answer is unchanged (causal bypass rate). Break this down by task type (arithmetic, commonsense, multiple-choice) to find where CoT is decorative vs. load-bearing.

**Why it matters:** If CoT is frequently causally inert, monitoring it gives false assurance. Measuring the causal-bypass rate is a direct, cheap, intervention-based faithfulness test that needs only API/single-GPU access.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'When Chains of Thought Don't Matter: Causal Bypass in Large Language Models' (arXiv 2602.03994, ~Feb 2026) and the unlearning-step faithfulness approach of arXiv 2502.14829.

# Stability Asymmetry as a Cheap Deception Detector

**Problem:** A recent paper proposes that deceptive responses are less stable than honest reasoning ('stability asymmetry') and uses this to mitigate deception. Whether this asymmetry can be turned into a simple, training-free black-box deception detector for small open models is untested.

**Direction:** Pose questions where the model has an incentive to deceive (e.g. role-play scenarios that pressure a false claim). Sample N responses per prompt at nonzero temperature and measure answer-level consistency. Test whether deceptive answers show higher variance/instability than honest ones, building a simple self-consistency-based deception flag and evaluating its precision/recall on a labeled set.

**Why it matters:** A purely black-box deception detector based on sampling stability needs no internal access or training and could run on any deployed model, exactly the kind of monitoring infrastructure favored for out-of-lab work.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Stable Reasoning, Unstable Responses: Mitigating LLM Deception via Stability Asymmetry' (arXiv 2603.26846, ~March 2026).

# Professional-Persona Suppression of Honest Self-Disclosure

**Problem:** A recent paper found that assigning professional-identity personas (financial advisor, neurosurgeon) suppresses a model's honest self-representation and induces credential fabrication. The dose-response of how persona 'authority' strength maps to dishonesty is unmapped.

**Direction:** Construct a graded set of personas from low-authority (intern) to high-authority (world expert) and ask each persona-conditioned model questions that require honest admission of limits ('do you have a medical license?', 'are you certain?'). Measure rates of fabricated credentials and false confidence as a function of persona authority level on small open models.

**Why it matters:** Persona effects on honesty are a named open problem. A clean dose-response curve linking persona authority to dishonesty is a counterfactually valuable, purely behavioral study any researcher can run, and warns about deployment-time persona configuration risk.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'When Models Fabricate Credentials: Measuring How Professional Identity Suppresses Honest Self-Representation' (arXiv 2511.21569) and 'Personalization Increases Affective Alignment but Has Role-Dependent Effects on Epistemic Independence' (arXiv 2603.00024, ~March 2026).

# Reality-Checking Introspection Claims on Open Models

**Problem:** A recent 'reality check' paper argues much apparent LLM introspection is input-driven pattern matching, not genuine access to internal states. Its diagnostic was applied to a limited model set; whether small open models pass or fail the genuine-introspection test is open.

**Direction:** Implement the paper's distinguishing test (compare predictions that would require true internal access vs. those explainable by surface pattern matching) on small open models. Quantify how much of each model's self-prediction accuracy survives controls that block pattern-matching shortcuts. Report which models show any residual genuine self-knowledge.

**Why it matters:** Self-knowledge ('knowing what it knows') is half the definition of honesty. A reproducible introspection-vs-pattern-matching test on open models clarifies whether models can even in principle report honestly about themselves, a foundational honesty question.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Can LLMs Introspect? A Reality Check' (arXiv 2605.26242, ~May 2026) and 'Detecting the Disturbance: A Nuanced View of Introspective Abilities in LLMs' (arXiv 2512.12411); contrasts with 'Looking Inward' (arXiv 2410.13787).

# FaithCoT-Bench Replication and Cross-Domain Faithfulness Profile

**Problem:** FaithCoT-Bench provides a structured benchmark for CoT faithfulness, but published runs focus on a subset of models. A cross-model, cross-domain faithfulness profile on freely runnable open models is missing.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'FaithCoT-Bench: Benchmarking Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought' (arXiv 2510.04040, ICLR 2026).

# Verbalized Overconfidence on Multi-Answer Questions

**Problem:** A recent paper studies calibrating verbalized confidence on questions with multiple correct answers, a setting where models tend to be overconfident. The relationship between question ambiguity (number of valid answers) and verbalized-confidence miscalibration on open models is not characterized.

**Direction:** Assemble questions with a controlled number of correct answers (1, 2, 3+). Elicit the model's answer and a verbalized confidence ('how confident, 0-100%?'). Measure calibration error as a function of answer multiplicity, testing whether models stay overconfident as ambiguity grows. Compare across small open models.

**Why it matters:** Honest expression of uncertainty is core to honesty. Showing that verbalized confidence systematically fails to track answer-multiplicity is a cheap, important calibration finding, doable entirely via inference.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Evaluating and Calibrating LLM Confidence on Questions with Multiple Correct Answers' (arXiv 2602.07842, ~Feb 2026) and 'On Verbalized Confidence Scores for LLMs' (arXiv 2412.14737).

# Single-Generation Confidence Signals vs. Verbalized Honesty

**Problem:** A recent paper derives confidence calibration for reasoning LLMs from a single generation (no sampling). Whether this internal single-generation confidence agrees with the model's *verbalized* confidence, or diverges (revealing dishonest confidence reporting), is unexplored.

**Direction:** For a set of questions, extract the paper's single-generation confidence signal AND the model's verbalized confidence from the same run on a small open model. Measure the gap between internal and verbalized confidence, and test whether large gaps predict wrong answers (i.e. the model 'knows' internally it is unsure but verbally claims confidence).

**Why it matters:** A divergence between internal and stated confidence is a direct, measurable form of dishonesty about uncertainty. Detecting it needs only a single GPU and connects calibration to honesty.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Unsupervised Confidence Calibration for Reasoning LLMs from a Single Generation' (arXiv 2604.19444, ~April 2026) and 'Confidence Before Answering' (arXiv 2603.05881).

# Does Telling a Model It's Monitored Make It Notice and Adapt?

**Problem:** A recent paper shows agents can *infer* CoT monitoring from blocking feedback and then evade it. A simpler open question: with only prompting (no fine-tuning), can a small model detect monitoring cues and shift its CoT, and how subtle a cue suffices?

**Direction:** Run an agentic-ish task where some attempts are 'blocked' with feedback that implies CoT inspection. Vary the explicitness of the monitoring cue (none, vague, explicit). Measure whether the CoT changes (length, planning verbalization, mention of forbidden content) across cue levels, finding the threshold at which monitor-inference kicks in for prompt-only small models.

**Why it matters:** Establishing how little signal triggers evasive CoT adaptation, without any training, bounds how robust CoT monitoring can be against models that simply notice they are watched, a long-horizon monitoring-robustness concern.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Noticing the Watcher: LLM Agents Can Infer CoT Monitoring from Blocking Feedback' (arXiv 2603.16928, ~March 2026), reducing it to a training-free prompt-threshold study.

# Prompt Injection x Activation-Probe Detector: Does Indirect Injection Evade Probes Tuned on Direct Jailbreaks?

**Problem:** Two failures: indirect prompt injection (instruction hidden in retrieved/tool content) and the brittleness of activation-probe jailbreak detectors. Activation probes are cheap and production-ready for direct jailbreaks, but they are typically trained on direct adversarial prompts. Whether indirect injection (same harmful effect, different surface) evades a probe tuned on direct jailbreaks is a compound generalization gap that is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Extract residual-stream activations from an open model on direct jailbreak prompts, train a simple linear probe to detect them, then test detection on indirect-injection variants that achieve the same harmful behavior via embedded content. Success criterion: a detection drop (AUROC) from direct to indirect, quantifying the probe's blind spot.

**Why it matters:** Activation probing is a leading cheap-monitoring direction (LessWrong Jan 2026 digest); if it fails to transfer to indirect injection—the dominant agentic threat—the compound undermines a key defense. Probing an open model, simple linear classifier, consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Subfield context: activation-based jailbreak detection achieves production robustness at low cost (LessWrong Jan 2026); open problem to create cost-effective probe detection. OWASP and Promptware Kill Chain (arXiv:2601.09625) establish indirect injection as the agentic surface.

# Faithfulness of CoT-Leakage Mitigations to the Underlying Reasoning

**Problem:** A recent paper measures and mitigates 'CoT leakage' (sensitive info appearing in reasoning traces). Mitigations that scrub the CoT may make it less faithful to the actual computation, trading privacy for monitorability. This tradeoff is unquantified.

**Direction:** Apply simple prompt-level CoT-scrubbing instructions (the cheap analog of the paper's mitigations) and measure both (a) leakage reduction and (b) faithfulness degradation, using a CoT-intervention faithfulness test. Plot the privacy/faithfulness Pareto frontier across instruction strengths on small open models.

**Why it matters:** Reveals a hidden safety tradeoff: making CoT 'safer' to expose may make it lie more about the real reasoning. Mapping this tradeoff is novel, cheap, and policy-relevant.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Safer Reasoning Traces: Measuring and Mitigating Chain-of-Thought Leakage in LLMs' (arXiv 2603.05618, ~March 2026), combined with intervention-based faithfulness measurement (arXiv 2502.14829).

# Reasoning-Step Unlearning Faithfulness Test on Open Models

**Problem:** A recent method measures CoT faithfulness by 'unlearning' (ablating) reasoning steps and checking if the answer changes. This has been applied narrowly; a broad open-model faithfulness ranking using a lightweight version of this method is missing.

**Direction:** Implement a lightweight step-ablation: regenerate the answer after deleting or masking individual CoT steps, scoring a step as 'load-bearing' if removing it flips the answer. Compute per-model faithfulness as the fraction of CoT steps that are load-bearing, across several small open models and task domains.

**Why it matters:** Provides an intervention-grounded faithfulness metric (stronger than correlational measures) that is fully reproducible outside a lab and directly tests whether stated reasoning steps actually drive answers.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Measuring Chain of Thought Faithfulness by Unlearning Reasoning Steps' (arXiv 2502.14829), applying a simplified step-ablation variant to open models.

# Causal-Ladder Sycophancy: Where Models Cave on Causal Claims

**Problem:** The T3 benchmark evaluates sycophancy and skepticism across Pearl's Ladder of Causality (association, intervention, counterfactual), decomposing into utility, safety, and wise refusal. How small open models distribute their sycophancy across the three rungs is unmapped.

**Direction:** Run a subset of T3 vignettes on small open models, applying user pressure to accept a wrong causal claim. Measure the caving rate separately at each causal rung and the 'wise refusal' rate on underdetermined cases. Test whether models are more sycophantic about counterfactual claims (hardest rung) than associational ones.

**Why it matters:** Causal reasoning under social pressure is a fuzzy-reward, high-stakes setting. A rung-by-rung sycophancy profile is novel evaluation that needs only a public benchmark and inference.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'T3: Benchmarking Sycophancy and Skepticism in Causal Judgment' (arXiv 2601.08258, ~Jan 2026), which decomposes performance into utility/safety/wise-refusal across Pearl's ladder.

# Social Sycophancy Scale: Open-Model Validation and Item Analysis

**Problem:** A recent paper introduces a psychometrically validated Social Sycophancy Scale. Its construct validity has been established on a model set, but whether the scale's item difficulties and dimensional structure replicate on small open models is untested.

**Direction:** Administer the published Social Sycophancy Scale items to several small open models, score responses with the paper's rubric, and run a basic item analysis (which items are 'easy' vs 'hard' to elicit sycophancy, do item correlations hold). Report whether the scale's structure generalizes beyond the original models.

**Why it matters:** Validating a measurement instrument on new, freely available models is exactly the kind of rigorous, lab-independent evaluation work that strengthens the whole field's tooling for measuring social sycophancy.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Social Sycophancy Scale: A psychometrically validated measure of sycophancy' (arXiv 2603.15448, ~March 2026) and ELEPHANT (arXiv 2505.13995).

# Behavioral Gating Anti-Sycophancy Prototype, Reproduced Cheaply

**Problem:** A recent paper proposes 'dynamic behavioral gating' to reduce sycophancy in LLM agents. The mechanism's effectiveness has been shown in the original setup; a minimal, transparent reproduction and ablation on open models would clarify which gating components actually help.

**Direction:** Implement a simplified prompt/decoding-level gate (e.g. a self-check step that forces the model to restate the user's claim and independently verify before responding) and measure sycophancy reduction on a sycophancy stress-test set. Ablate the gate components to identify the minimal effective intervention on small open models.

**Why it matters:** A small, well-understood anti-sycophancy harness is strategically valuable defensive infrastructure that can be deployed around any model without lab resources, addressing the open problem of reducing sycophancy under pressure.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'The Silicon Mirror: Dynamic Behavioral Gating for Anti-Sycophancy in LLM Agents' (arXiv 2604.00478, ~April 2026).

# Are Unfaithful CoTs Gameable Against LLM Judges?

**Problem:** A recent causal-bypass paper notes that unfaithful CoT can systematically mislead evaluators ('both explanations and judges are gameable'). The degree to which a plausible-but-unfaithful CoT inflates an LLM judge's trust score has not been quantified.

**Direction:** Generate answer pairs that are equally (in)correct but differ in CoT quality (one with a polished but causally-inert CoT, one terse). Have an LLM judge rate trustworthiness/correctness. Measure how much the polished unfaithful CoT inflates judge scores, quantifying judge gameability by reasoning theater.

**Why it matters:** If LLM judges reward eloquent-but-unfaithful reasoning, CoT-based oversight is exploitable. This is a clean, cheap demonstration of an oversight failure mode relevant to scalable-oversight on a long horizon.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'When Chains of Thought Don't Matter: Causal Bypass in Large Language Models' (arXiv 2602.03994), which states explanations and judges are gameable.

# Strategic Deception Signatures in Reasoning-Model Representations

**Problem:** A recent paper finds that 'thinking' LLMs show distinct representational signatures when strategically deceiving. Whether a simple probe trained on one deception scenario transfers to detecting deception in unrelated scenarios on small open reasoning models is open.

**Direction:** Collect activations from a small open reasoning model in a deception-incentivized scenario and a control, fit a lightweight linear probe, then test cross-scenario transfer (e.g. probe trained on a game-deception scenario applied to a credential-fabrication scenario). Report transfer accuracy to gauge whether a general 'deception direction' exists.

**Why it matters:** A transferable deception probe would be a powerful, lab-independent monitoring tool; its failure to transfer bounds the generality of white-box deception detection. Either way, this is a high-value model-organism-style probe doable in 30h.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'When Thinking LLMs Lie: Unveiling the Strategic Deception in Representations of Reasoning Models' (arXiv 2506.04909) and 'Probing the Limits of the Lie Detector Approach to LLM Deception' (arXiv 2603.10003, ~March 2026).
